problem: Earlier embodied vision-language tasks fall short of how people actually give robots tasks. R2R/VLN uses long step-by-step navigation instructions and judges only point navigation. EQA judges only a QA answer. Referring-expression datasets such as RefCOCO ground an object in a single static image. None of them tests an agent that follows a short, high-level command to find and localise a remote object that is not visible from the start in an unseen real building.
motivation: Practical robot commands are concise and object-centric, e.g. 'bring me the pillow from my bedroom'. Carrying them out needs semantic priors about where things are, navigation without detailed guidance, and object grounding among many candidates seen from varying viewpoints. The authors show that simply chaining state-of-the-art VLN navigators with the MAttNet referring-expression model fails badly: FAST-Short SPL drops from 43% on R2R val-unseen to 6.17% on REVERIE val-unseen. This motivates both a new benchmark and a model in which the navigator and the pointer inform each other.
key_idea: Introduce REVERIE, a benchmark of 21,702 short, high-level remote-object instructions built on the Matterport3D simulator extended with projected object bounding boxes, together with an Interactive Navigator-Pointer baseline. In this baseline, the referring-expression pointer's top-3 matched objects per candidate view (their category labels and region features) are fed into a FAST-short navigator as hard attention.
insight: Navigation, not grounding, is the bottleneck. At the ground-truth goal viewpoint MAttNet reaches 48.98% test accuracy (Table 4, RefExp-only). Chaining it with the best navigator (FAST-Short) gives only 7.07% REVERIE success. Letting pointer outputs guide navigation raises test navigation SR from 14.18 to 19.88 and REVERIE success from 7.07 to 11.28; FAST-Short is described as the ablation without the interaction module. So object-level grounding cues are more informative for goal-directed navigation than whole-view features when instructions are high-level. A FAST-Lan-Only control, which sees no visual input, gets high oracle success but very low SR/SPL, showing the dataset has little pure language bias.
method: Task/simulator extension: Matterport3D object annotations (centre, 3 axis directions, 3 radii) are converted to 8 vertices and projected into each viewpoint/camera view. Occlusion is handled by bbox overlap plus depth, and only objects within 3 m of a viewpoint are kept, giving about 20k object annotations. The agent picks nav-graph viewpoints and outputs one bounding box (or picks from simulator candidates) exactly once per episode.

Dataset: AMT workers watched a path animation to a highlighted target object and wrote free-form high-level commands, 3 per object. Result: 21,702 instructions averaging 18 words, 4,140 target objects in 489 categories, 90 buildings, and R2R-style train/val-seen/val-unseen/test splits.

Navigator: a FAST-short seq2seq LSTM using the SelfMonitor visual-textual co-grounding (positional-encoded textual attention and visual attention over K candidate views) plus a progress monitor. Candidate logits are an inner product of W_a[h_t, x̂_t] with g(v'_{t,k}). Search keeps a candidate queue and an ending queue with accumulated logits and backtracks; the stop is the visited viewpoint with the highest accumulated logit.

Pointer: MAttNet decomposes the instruction into subject, location and relationship phrase embeddings. Each object gets modular matching scores from 2-layer MLPs, combined by a language-predicted softmax weighting.

Interaction module: for each candidate viewpoint, the pointer selects its top-3 matching objects. Their category labels are encoded by a bi-LSTM and their ResNet FC7 region features are averaged. Both are concatenated to the view feature (v' ∈ R^4736) and fed to the navigator, so the pointer acts as hard attention over target-related objects.

Losses: navigation loss is cross-entropy on actions plus MSE on the progress monitor (λ1=0.5). The referring loss is a bidirectional triplet ranking loss over (object, expression) negatives. They are summed as L = L_nav + λ4·L_exp. In practice the pointer is trained first on goal-viewpoint views, then the navigator is trained with the pointer's object cues.

setting.backbone: LSTM seq2seq navigator (FAST-short / SelfMonitor co-grounding, ResNet image features) + MAttNet pointer, trained on REVERIE
setting.training_data: REVERIE train split only: 59 scenes, 10,466 instructions, 2,353 target objects. The pointer is trained on goal-viewpoint views containing the target in MAttNet format; no extra/web data.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views: 12 headings × 3 elevations) + navigable viewpoints + simulator-provided object bounding boxes/candidates
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (with FAST backtracking search) + a single object-selection / bounding-box output
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator (extended with projected object bounding boxes)
setting.privileged: candidate object bounding boxes and category labels projected from Matterport3D GT object annotations are provided at test time (part of the task definition); no GT goal location

numbers_note: This is the original CVPR 2020 version. It reports REVERIE success (IoU≥0.5 / correct candidate, here mapped to RGS) but no RGSPL; later leaderboards add RGSPL. The printed SPL of 45.50 in Table 3 is written as 45.5 here. Table 3 also contains baseline and human rows (human test: SR 81.51, OSR 86.83, SPL 53.66, TL 21.18, REVERIE Succ. 77.84), which are not listed as own numbers. Table 4 gives an oracle 'referring expression only' setting at the GT goal viewpoint (MAttNet 68.45/56.63/48.98, CM-Erase 65.21/54.02/45.25, CNN-RNN baseline 30.69/18.63/16.18, human test 90.76); these are baseline models, not the paper's own method.
results: The Interactive Navigator-Pointer is the best non-human method on every split. Test navigation SR is 19.88 and SPL 11.61, and REVERIE success is 11.28, beating the strongest pipeline baseline, FAST-Short+MAttNet (14.18 SR / 8.74 SPL / 7.07 REVERIE success), by 4.2 points of REVERIE success. It remains far below human performance (77.84% REVERIE success on test). Even with the agent placed at the GT goal viewpoint, SoTA referring-expression models reach only about 49% on test, versus about 80% on RefCOCO.
limitations: Absolute performance is very low (7.84% RGS on val-unseen) with a large seen/unseen gap. FAST backtracking also produces very long trajectories (45 m TL on val-unseen) and poor SPL.

Relies on simulator-provided object candidate boxes and labels projected from GT Matterport3D annotations rather than a detector. The pointer and navigator are trained in stages, with no true end-to-end joint optimisation or feedback from navigator to pointer.
The agent may output an object only once per episode, and navigation success is defined loosely (target within 3 m), so navigation metrics are not directly comparable to R2R.
